overview: This file brings together two related strands of early occupation policy concerning precious assets in Japan. The first is an exchange between New York attorney James F. Dulligan and the State Department about whether diamonds and other rare stones seized by U.S. occupation forces would be sold publicly; Edwin M. Martin replies that some might be looted property and that their disposition awaited Far Eastern Commission policy. The second strand concerns a War Department proposal to revise SCAP reporting on precious metals by distinguishing ownership, custody, national origin, and evidence of looting, while reducing reports from monthly to quarterly. State Department annotations and the final reply add detailed reporting requirements for coins and other monetary and non-monetary metals, reflecting interest in assaying the stocks and possibly using them to finance Japanese foreign trade.

subfiles.title: Dulligan inquiry about the sale of diamonds seized in Japan
subfiles.to: Edwin Martin, Japanese-Korean Economic Affairs Commission, Department of State
subfiles.about: A New York attorney asks when diamonds and other rare stones seized by the U.S. Army in Japan will be offered for public sale.
subfiles.summary: Dulligan writes on behalf of a client interested in purchasing diamonds, jewelry, and other rare stones seized by American forces in Japan. Believing that the assets are intended for sale, he requests information about whether and when they will become available to the public.

subfiles.title: Martin reply on the disposition of impounded precious stones
subfiles.from: Edwin M. Martin, Chief, Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs
subfiles.about: Martin explains that SCAP has not authorized the export or sale of impounded gems and that their disposition depends on forthcoming Far Eastern Commission policy.
subfiles.summary: Martin states that precious gems impounded by the occupation authorities have not been included in SCAP's export program. Because many items may have been looted from territories formerly occupied by Japan, their disposition must await policies established by the Far Eastern Commission. He promises appropriate publicity if those policies eventually permit sales in the United States.

subfiles.title: Chard transmittal of proposed precious-metals reporting letter
subfiles.from: Colonel R. H. Chard, Executive, Civil Affairs Division, War Department
subfiles.to: Assistant Secretary of State for Occupied Areas, attention W. M. Cameron
subfiles.about: Chard requests State Department comments on a draft letter revising SCAP's reports on precious metals in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Chard transmits a proposed letter to SCAP for review by the State Department. He explains that the reporting system, recently discussed with Mr. McDiarmid, would be placed on a quarterly basis and revised to provide more complete information about ownership of the reported metals.

subfiles.title: Proposed letter to SCAP on reports of precious metals in Japan
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: The draft directs SCAP to expand and reorganize its reporting on precious-metal stocks by ownership, custody, origin, and possible looting.
subfiles.summary: The proposed letter replaces the existing monthly procedure with quarterly reports and requests coverage of metals both in and outside SCAP custody. Metals in custody are to be divided among known Japanese-owned stocks, assets earmarked for non-Japanese interests, and holdings of unidentified ownership, with further distinctions based on country of origin and evidence of looting. The draft also requests progress reports on assaying, notes Treasury interest in that issue, and changes the report's control symbol to WDSCA-5.

subfiles.title: Handwritten note on classification of non-SCAP metal stocks
subfiles.to: Action officer; instruction to call McCormick of the Civil Affairs Division
subfiles.about: The note recommends a more detailed division of precious-metal stocks outside SCAP custody.
subfiles.summary: The annotation directs that McCormick of the Civil Affairs Division be called. It proposes dividing non-SCAP stocks into monetary and non-monetary holdings, separating coins from other monetary metals, and reporting coins by principal metallic content, face value, and weight.

subfiles.title: State Department routing note for McDiarmid's review
subfiles.from: Office of the Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Division of Japanese and Korean Economic Affairs; Orville J. McDiarmid
subfiles.about: The routing annotation sends the proposed reporting changes to McDiarmid for action, comment, and concurrence by a July 18 suspense date.
subfiles.summary: The sheet routes the matter to the Japanese and Korean economic-affairs staff and specifically to McDiarmid. A further annotation asks Mr. Jerabely to refer it to McDiarmid for comment and concurrence, with July 18 recorded as the suspense date.

subfiles.title: Hilldring reply proposing detailed reporting of metals outside SCAP custody
subfiles.from: J. H. Hilldring, Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Colonel R. H. Chard, Executive, Civil Affairs Division, War Department
subfiles.about: Hilldring recommends that SCAP provide detailed classifications and valuations of monetary and non-monetary metals outside its custody.
subfiles.summary: Hilldring endorses an expansion of the proposed report because officials were considering using Japan's precious-metal stocks to help finance foreign trade. For coins, he requests principal metallic content, issuing country, weight, face value, dollar value, and approximate date of issue. Other monetary metals and non-monetary metals are to be reported by type of metal, weight, and dollar value.

interest: The file is valuable because it connects the restitution problem posed by potentially looted gems with the occupation authorities' broader management of Japan's gold and precious-metal reserves. Its proposed reporting taxonomy preserves unusually detailed distinctions among governmental, banking, corporate, private, foreign, unidentified, and demonstrably looted holdings. The annotations and final reply also show policy being formed through interdepartmental review and reveal that these assets were being considered not merely for custody or restitution but as a possible means of financing Japan's postwar foreign trade.
